Judith lifted her voice to the great Lord, besides whom there is no other, and glorified Him, because His power is above every power and He is the Creator of all things; so it is natural that all creatures should worship Him.

entries.section: (1) The hymn of Judith

paragraphs.text: Even if nature appears lofty, in the form of its mountains and mighty towering rocks and its huge, deep seas, all of it shakes and melts like wax before the face of God, as the same meaning is repeated in (Mic 1:4, Ps 97:5).
If lifeless nature, which has no reason, submits to God, how much more should you, O man, worship God faithfully and glorify Him at all times.
Praise God in His power and meditate on His creation, that you may fear Him, and so reject sin and walk faithfully before Him.

entries.section: (1) The hymn of Judith

paragraphs.text: Honored: dear and esteemed.

From the foregoing it clearly appears that God magnifies everyone who worships Him, fears Him and trusts in Him, for the Jews were exalted above all the power of the Assyrians, because they are the people of God who worship Him.
In proportion as you worship God with faith and faithfulness, the Lord gives you favor in the eyes of men and happiness on earth, and then glory that cannot be expressed in the heavens.

entries.section: (1) The hymn of Judith

paragraphs.text: How wretched is the one who opposes the children of God, for he opposes God Himself, and many troubles await him on earth and eternal torment in heaven, which Judith described as the torment of fire and worms, as the Holy Bible affirms in many places (Sir 7:19; Isa 14:11; Mk 9:44). The expression "fire and worms" is a figure of what happens in eternal torment, where the worm keeps eating them and the fire keeps burning in them for ever. There is no material worm or fire, but something far more severe, for it is spiritual, and the torment has no end. Judith uses the expression "worms and fire" because it was known among the Jews in a valley called the Valley of Hinnom, which lies south of Jerusalem, where the remains and carcasses of animals were thrown and burned with fire. Because of the large number of carcasses, the fire kept burning in this valley, and at the edges of the valley the worms kept eating these carcasses. From it came the word Gehenna, because valley in Hebrew = Ge and Hinnom is the name of this valley, so Ge + Hinnom = Gehenna.

Thus the conditions were reversed: the children of Israel, who were faint from thirst and hunger, became strong, and by the power of God triumphed over the mighty Assyrians, despite their strength, their weapons and their huge numbers. The giants fled like children before the power of God in His people.

Do not oppress the weak or break the commandments of God, lest many afflictions come upon you in this life. And if they come upon you, hasten to repentance, that God may deliver you from eternal torment.

entries.section: (2) Presenting gifts to the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: After the people of Bethulia had celebrated the victory of the Lord over the Assyrians by the hand of Judith and by their own hands, they did not forget to go to Jerusalem, where the temple of God was, to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and burnt offerings of praise to God, and to present all their vows and what they had promised God during their affliction.

It is good to pray to God in your chamber (Bethulia), but do not forget the dwelling of God (His temple), that is, the holy Church, where God dwells in a special way through the Holy Sacraments and unites with His people. God rejoices in you and welcomes your coming to Him, to visit Him in His house, that is, the Church.

In proportion to the prayers they had lifted up during their affliction was the expression of their thanks to God after their victory, in the celebrations of Bethulia and in their visit to Jerusalem to present the holy offerings.
Does thanksgiving have a sufficient place in your prayers and your life? Or are the requests many and the thanks few after the requests are fulfilled?

entries.section: (2) Presenting gifts to the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: Ibsal nisyan: a Hebrew expression meaning a perpetual dedication, or something forbidden for anyone to take and set apart for God. In the translation of the Jesuit Fathers it is rendered "I offered it to God as a ban," that is, I set it apart, and none of the people or the rulers can take it for ever. In the English translation, "Votive offering to God." As for Judith, whom they had singled out with the most precious of the spoils, the belongings of the commander Holofernes, and who accepted them with thanks from her people, she put under ban everything she had acquired of the spoils, that is, she consecrated it to God, to remain in the house of God throughout the generations as a proof of the power of God and His care for His people, together with the war equipment of Holofernes, that is, his dagger and his weapon and the canopy of the bed, that is, the mosquito net that protects him from insects, which, in spite of his might, could not protect him from the hand of God. All these things remained in the temple of God, as a proof of the weakness of the wicked before the greatness of God. Thus we see that Judith took nothing for herself in return for her labor and her accomplishing the victory, because she believes that God alone accomplished the victory, and He alone deserves to be honored and to have gifts presented to Him, and because she is a detached person who lives devoted to God in a life of solitude, a stranger to the world and its possessions.

It is beautiful to remind yourself of everything that helps you grow in your spiritual life: crosses, icons of the saints and every blessing you bring from the holy places stir your feelings if they grow cold, and you become attached to God.

entries.section: (2) Presenting gifts to the house of the Lord

paragraphs.text: There was great joy for all the people of Bethulia who came with Judith to Jerusalem when they saw the holy places, and they continued for three months celebrating before God with thanksgiving, joy and many acts of worship in the temple. The number three represents the perfection of the work of the Holy Trinity in man, that is, they gave God the opportunity to work in them with all His power.

Would that we celebrate our feasts in a spiritual way, with greater attachment to the Church, the prayers, the readings and works of mercy, instead of being absorbed in material pleasures of food and clothing.

entries.section: (3) The greatness of Judith and her repose

paragraphs.text: More glorious: from glory, meaning greater.

The people of Bethulia returned to their city with joy after three months and lived in their houses, and Judith returned to her house and went up to her upper room to continue her life of solitude, prayers and praise to God in strict asceticism. She was not occupied with the praise of men and their honoring, because the goal of her life is the love of God. She did not appear except at the spiritual feasts, to share with her people in the worship of God, and her glory and greatness appeared as a blessed saint, living with God night and day.

If the circumstances of your life and your occupations change, or you travel to the right or to the left, return afterward with zeal to your spiritual life and your usual rule, and do not let the occupations of life hinder you so that you grow cold in your worship, because the goal of our life is one, and it is the love of God.

The most important virtues of Judith - which appeared in her victory over Holofernes and continued throughout her life - were the virtue of courage, built on faith in God and self-sacrifice, in addition to the virtue of chastity, for she was content with widowhood after her husband, to live consecrated to God, although it is logical that many of the great would desire to marry her, especially after the victory accomplished by her hand, but she insisted on consecrating her life to God, preferring Him to union with any human being.

To acquire the virtue of chastity, be content with what you have and thank God, and try to see God in all the material things you have, and give up as much as you can, by detachment from the material things to which your heart clings.

entries.section: (3) The greatness of Judith and her repose

paragraphs.text: God granted Judith a long life in solitude, and she lived one hundred and five years, exactly as the father of all monks, the great saint Anba Anthony, lived. Perhaps her life was one of the examples of the life of solitude in the Old Testament, and a preparation for the appearance of the systems of communal monasticism, which began at the hands of St. Anba Anthony.

Thus Judith appears as a great saint, one of the most famous holy women who appeared in the Old Testament, bearing many virtues, the most important cause of which was perhaps her tasting of fellowship with God in the life of solitude. Since she lived a life of detachment and kept none of the spoils of the Assyrians, she continued in a life of giving, and so she set her maidservant free, and this was a blessing from God to this faithful maidservant, who took part in bringing salvation to the people of God. She is a symbol of Joseph of Arimathea, or Nicodemus, or Mary Magdalene, or Simon of Cyrene, to whom God gave a blessing because of their share in the crucifixion of Christ, His burial and the placing of spices on His body.

God blesses the smallest work you offer Him as a share in His love; even if it is only a cup of cold water, or two mites, or five loaves and two fishes, its reward will not be lost. So offer God what you have, in worship and service, however small it may seem, for it is very precious in the eyes of God.

entries.section: (3) The greatness of Judith and her repose

paragraphs.text: When Judith died, who was honored not only by the people of her city but by all the Jews, they grieved greatly for her and made a mourning for her for seven days. The number seven points to perfection, that is, the perfection of grief at her departure. The number seven also symbolizes the Holy Spirit, for at the end of the seven days they received comfort from God. Their mourning for her for seven days shows that they regarded her as one of the famous of the Jews, and in this mourning joys and celebrations are suspended.

entries.section: (3) The greatness of Judith and her repose

paragraphs.text: Among the blessings of God to His people for the sake of Judith is that no wars or attacks by the nations arose against the Jews during the whole life of Judith, and even for a time after her death.

God has mercy on His people for the sake of His saints. May you be righteous, and God will keep your family, your relatives and those you serve in the Church of your children, for the sake of your love for Him. And let you have friendship with the saints, and God will have mercy on you for the sake of their prayers.

entries.section: (3) The greatness of Judith and her repose

paragraphs.text: The day of the killing of Holofernes by the hand of Judith and the attack of the Jews on the camp of the Assyrians became a feast for the Jews through the years, in which they glorify the great God who triumphs over His enemies, rescues His people from afflictions and works in the humble who trust in Him. To this day the Jews still keep this feast on the twenty-fifth day of the month of December, and they read the Book of Judith in it.
Judith offered three prayers on different occasions. We mention here what each prayer contained:
A - Her prayer in her chamber before she undertook her mission (ch. 9:2-19).
1- Her knowledge of the God of her father, who is the God of heaven and the helper in afflictions (vv. 2-5).
2- Her humility and her confession of her weakness (vv. 3, 15, 17).
3- Her faith that God answers her prayer (v. 17).
4- Her trust in the mercy of God (v. 17).
5- Her remembering the former works of God and asking for His intervention (vv. 6-11).
6- Her asking for the destruction of the power of the enemies (v. 11).
7- Her asking that God rescue His temple (v. 11).
8- Her asking for help to carry out her plan (vv. 13, 14).
9- Her asking that the name of God be magnified above all gods (v. 19).
B - Her prayer in the tent of Holofernes immediately before killing him (ch. 13:7).
1- Her asking for help from God, the God of her people.
2- She reminded God of His promises to rescue His people if they took refuge in Him.
3- Her confidence in the power of God, which supports her until she completes her plan.
C - Her hymn in her city after the victory (ch. 16:2-21).
1- Her asking the people to glorify God with musical instruments (v. 2).
2- Proclaiming the power of God who triumphs in wars (v. 3).
3- God dwells in the midst of His people and protects them (v. 4).
4- God, who mocks the power of the enemies and their threats and kills them by the hand of the weak (vv. 5-8).
5- Holofernes' falling into lust, Judith, so she killed him with his dagger (vv. 9-11).
6- The fear of the Assyrians and their flight before the people of God (vv. 12-14).
7- Praise of God, who is able to do all things and is glorified by all His creatures (vv. 15-18).
8- The Lord honors His people (v. 19).
9- God takes vengeance on the enemies of His people and casts them into eternal torment (vv. 20, 21). The similarity of the prayers in these points is to be noted:
1- Glorifying God, who is able to do all things and who has been victorious from of old.
2- Confession of weakness and need of God's help.
3- Confidence in the power of God, which destroys the enemies and protects His people.

A summary of the life of Judith in lines. (1) Judith was the widow of a husband named Manasseh, who died of sunstroke during the barley harvest (Jdt 8:2, 3, 7). (2) She had remained a widow for three years and six months (Jdt 8:4). (3) She lived in a room at the top of her house with her maidservants (Jdt 8:5). (4) She lived a life of austerity and asceticism, fasting and wearing sackcloth all the days of her life, except on the Sabbaths and the feasts (Jdt 8:6). (5) She was very beautiful in appearance and very rich, and she had a reputation among all people that she feared the Lord (Jdt 8:7, 8), and she was distinguished by many virtues, the most important of which were chastity (Jdt 10:4), courage (Jdt 16:26) and wisdom (Jdt 8:28). (6) When she heard that Uzziah, the ruler of the city of Bethulia, had set a delay of five days, and that if God did not rescue them within it he would surrender the city, she intervened and warned them not to tempt God by setting a time limit for His intervention (Jdt 8:9-12). (7) She asked for the prayers of the elders of the city, that God might help her to carry out her plan to rescue her people (Jdt 8:30-34). (8) She prayed, then adorned herself and went out with her maidservant from Bethulia, and the Assyrians seized her and delivered her to Holofernes, who was captivated by her beauty. She stayed with him three days, and he had permitted her to eat of her own food which she had brought with her and to wash in the water of the springs of Bethulia, to complete her worship and prayers (Jdt 10). (9) At the end of the three days Holofernes called her to his tent, and she went to him after he had drunk much wine and lost consciousness, and she drew his dagger and cut off his head and wrapped it in the mosquito net of his bed. She and her maidservant went out and went to Bethulia, bringing them the good news of victory (Jdt 12:10-13). (10) She asked the people to hang the head of Holofernes on the wall, and then each one to take his weapon, making an uproar as if intending to attack the Assyrians, so that the spies would go to inform their chief Holofernes and find him killed, and terror would fall on them; then they would swoop down on the Assyrians and have the victory by the power of God (Jdt 14:1-5). (11) The Jews carried out what Judith asked, and the Assyrians fled from the face of the Jews, who pursued them to the borders of Syria and took their baggage and spoils for thirty days. They gave Judith all the possessions of Holofernes, as a memorial of what she had done for them, and she in turn gave these things to the temple of the Lord as a perpetual dedication (Jdt 14:6-15:8). (12) Judith praised God and completed her life in solitude, and did not know a man, and set her maidservant free, and remained in the house of her husband 105 years, and died and was buried beside her husband in Bethulia, and the people mourned for her seven days (Jdt 16:26-31). Symbols of Christ and the Church. Judith is a symbol of the Church. Judith was distinguished by many virtues which are essential characteristics of the Church, with which the faithful in every generation should be adorned, the most important of which are:
1- Obedience to the commandments of God:

Judith took care to carry out the Law, in observing the Sabbaths and the feasts, the washing, and keeping to the eating of clean foods. Her commitment was continuous throughout her life, even in the time of affliction, when she lived with the enemies (Jdt 8:6, 12:2).
2- Prayer and fasting:

Judith lived holding fast to prayers and fasts, especially after her widowhood, for she withdrew into an upper room inside her house, and she fasted and prayed and wore sackcloth. She fasted until the evening and ate only clean foods, as the Law requires, leaving the other foods which the Gentiles eat, and she held fast to her fasts and prayers even when her circumstances were difficult during her stay with Holofernes (Jdt 12:7-9).
3- Faith:

She believed in God who saves His people in her city, Bethulia, and she refused the fixing of a time within which God should work to rescue His people, the five days, for this is a tempting of God - and this is not right - and she asked those in charge of the city to trust in God, and she believed that He would save their city within the time they had set, and this is a faith that surpasses reason (Jdt 8:9-34).
4- Chastity:

Judith lived seven years with her husband, then became a widow and remained chaste and devoted to God, although she was very beautiful and rich, and it would have been easy for her to marry a second time.
5- The life of solitude:

Judith is an image of the love of solitude and monasticism in the Old Testament, for after her widowhood she lived as though she were a nun in her cell, which was an upper room in her house, and she gave up the enjoyment of the delights of the house and devoted herself to prayer, gave up delicious foods and lived in asceticism (Jdt 8:5). But she left her solitude for the good of her people and went out to meet Holofernes, destroyed him and saved her people, just as the great saint Anba Anthony, the father of the monks, came out from his solitude in the wilderness to fight the heresy of Arius and to support the faith of Pope Athanasius, so that the people would be established in the faith.
6- Self-giving:
Judith is an example of martyrdom in her going out to meet the hard-hearted Holofernes, exposing her life to danger, but God delivered her; she is a martyr without the shedding of blood.
7- Praise:

She expressed her joy in the way she had been accustomed to throughout her life, which is prayer and praise, for when she triumphed over Holofernes and saved her people she praised God (Jdt 13:20-22, 16:1-17).
8- Giving:
Judith was ascetic in her life, so when the people gave her the private belongings of Holofernes and his tent, she gave them as a gift to the temple in Jerusalem (Jdt 16:23).
9- Acceptance of the Gentiles:

Judith took care to call Achior to the faith, when she told him of the death of Holofernes and showed him his head, and he was so amazed that he lost consciousness, and afterward he declared his faith, he and his household, and joined the people of God.
10- Humility:

Which appeared in her prayers (Jdt 9, 16) and in her asking her people to pray for her before carrying out her plan to rescue her city (Jdt 18:31, 33), her bowing down before Holofernes for the sake of God (Jdt 10:20), then her ascribing the victory and all the glory to God (Jdt 13:27). And her going to Jerusalem to bow down before the temple of God (Jdt 16:22).
